teaser: Buried by a landslide, saved from the furnace: a bronze driver who still has his eyes.
review_notes:
Discovery in spring 1896 in two main parts, by the French excavation led by Théophile Homolle: standard account; no quote is attributed.
Relocation of the village of Kastri before the dig: standard account.
Burial by the earthquake and rockfall of 373 BC: standard account.
Dedication by Polyzalos of Gela for a Pythian victory (478 or 474 BC): based on the inscribed base; the reading of the inscription is debated.
Eye inlays (glass and stone), copper on lips and eyelashes, silver on the headband pattern and teeth: commonly reported, exact materials vary by source.
Height about 1.80 m.
The idea that the long lower body corrects for a low viewpoint or for the hidden chariot box is a common hypothesis, not a certainty.
The photo is taken from below and slightly to the statue's right; the lost left arm is on the right side of the image.

lesson.text: In the spring of 1896, French archaeologists digging at Delphi, in central Greece, hit metal. First came the lower half of a robed figure. A few days later, a short distance away, the upper half appeared, with the head still attached. The diggers could hardly believe one detail: the statue was looking back at them. Its eyes were intact.

Their amazement made sense. The ancient Greeks cast thousands of life-size bronzes, and almost all are gone. Bronze is valuable, so later centuries melted statues down for coins, tools and weapons. What we usually see in museums are Roman copies in marble. An original bronze from the 400s BC is a rare survivor.

To excavate Delphi, an entire village had to be moved. The houses of Kastri stood right on top of the ancient sanctuary, and its inhabitants were relocated to a new site nearby before the dig could begin in 1892.

The driver owes his survival to a disaster. In 373 BC an earthquake sent rocks crashing down the mountain onto the sanctuary. The monument was smashed and covered with earth. Nobody could reach it to recycle it. The ground kept it for more than two thousand years.

He stands about 1.80 m tall (5 ft 11 in), and he was never meant to stand alone. He drove a bronze chariot pulled by four bronze horses, of which only scraps were found. Start at the top, with the part that astonished the excavators.

lesson.title: A face with its colors
lesson.text: Greek bronzes were not one color. Other materials were set into the metal.

spots.title: The eyes
spots.text: The whites and dark irises are separate pieces of glass and stone fixed into the sockets. Most ancient bronzes have lost theirs and stare with empty holes.

spots.title: The victor's band
spots.text: A flat ribbon is tied around the head, the mark of a winner. Its geometric pattern was once picked out in silver.

spots.title: Curls at the temple
spots.text: Below the band, small locks curl in front of the ear, as if damp with sweat. Over the skull the hair lies flat and neat.

spots.title: The mouth
spots.text: The full lips are slightly parted and were covered in reddish copper. The jaw is heavy, the expression gives almost nothing away.

lesson.text: Picture the statue new. The bronze was not green but a warm golden brown, like tanned skin. Against it: red lips, bright eyes, a glinting headband. The green you see today is a crust formed by centuries underground.

Who was he? A base found with the statue names the man who paid: Polyzalos, ruler of the Greek city of Gela in Sicily. His team won the chariot race at the Pythian Games, held at Delphi in honor of the god Apollo. In Greek racing the glory went to the owner of the horses. The driver was a hired professional, and his name is lost.

A statue this size was not poured in one go. The Charioteer was cast in several separate pieces, including the head, the arms, the upper body and the long skirt, which were then joined together. The seams hide under the belt and the sleeves.

The sculptor did not choose the thunder of the race. This is afterward: the slow parade before the crowd, reins held loosely. That calm belongs to a short period historians call the Severe Style, around 480 to 450 BC, when Greek artists gave up the fixed smile of older statues for serious faces and simple, weighty shapes. The robe shows it best.
The long tunic of a racing driver, read as three lines.

lines.label: The high belt
lines.text: The robe is cinched well above the natural waist. Everything below becomes one very long skirt, which makes the figure look taller and stiller.

lines.label: The column
lines.text: The folds drop straight down in deep parallel grooves, like the fluting on a temple column. Yet no two folds are quite alike.

lines.label: The reins
lines.text: Thin bronze straps still hang from the right hand and trail down across the skirt. They once ran forward to four horses.

lesson.text: Those long legs can look odd up close. One common explanation: the skirt was half hidden by the front of the chariot, and the whole group stood on a high base, seen from below. Notice also that he is not perfectly frontal. Feet, hips, chest and head each turn a little further to one side, a slow twist that keeps the column alive.

spots.title: The sleeve
spots.text: On the shoulder and upper arm the cloth gathers into fine, rippling pleats, quite different from the straight grooves of the skirt.

spots.title: The right hand
spots.text: Fingers curl around the straps with an easy grip. The forearm is bare and smooth, held out level in front of the body.

spots.title: The missing arm
spots.text: On this side the sleeve ends in an empty opening. The left arm, cast separately, was never found.

spots.title: The neckline
spots.text: The tunic opens in a V below a long, strong neck. Folds fan out from it across the chest.

spots.title: The feet
spots.text: Bare, with long toes and carefully modeled bones. They are among the most lifelike parts of the statue, though hardly anyone in the crowd could have seen them.

lesson.text: Chariot racing was the most expensive sport in the Greek world, a contest between rulers and millionaires. Because the prize went to the owner, a person could win without even attending the race.

So the richest part of the monument, the tyrant's proud gift with its horses and chariot, is rubble. What the mountain kept is the employee, the one person nobody thought to name. He has now been looking out over visitors for longer than he ever looked out over the sanctuary.

quiz.question: Why are original Greek bronze statues so rare?
options: Most were melted down for their metal
The Greeks made very few of them
quiz.explanation: Bronze was valuable and later ages recycled statues into coins, tools and weapons.

quiz.question: What saved the Charioteer?
options: Priests hid it in a temple
An earthquake and rockfall buried it in 373 BC
quiz.explanation: Buried under rubble, it could not be reached and melted.

quiz.question: Who received the glory of a chariot victory?
options: The city where the race was held
quiz.explanation: The prize went to the owner, here Polyzalos of Gela, not to the hired driver.

quiz.question: What are the eyes made of?
quiz.explanation: Separate pieces of glass and stone were set into the sockets.

quiz.question: What marks the Severe Style?
options: Serious faces and simple, weighty shapes
quiz.explanation: Around 480 to 450 BC artists dropped the old fixed smile for calm gravity.

facts.text: The Charioteer originally stood alone, without horses.
facts.explanation: He was part of a group with a chariot and four horses, of which only fragments survive.

facts.text: When new, the bronze was golden brown, not green.
facts.explanation: The green surface is a crust formed during centuries underground.

facts.text: The statue was cast in a single piece.
facts.explanation: It was cast in several parts that were joined, with seams hidden under belt and sleeves.
